While Apple has done its best to protect Jony Ive in its lawsuit against OpenAI, the company may not be able to keep its former design chief out of the dispute. Here's why.

OpenAI has the chance to put Apple in an awkward spot

In its lawsuit accusing OpenAI of stealing trade secrets, Apple has deliberately avoided naming Jony Ive. His company, io Products, previously collaborated with OpenAI to develop the hardware products at the centre of the case.

In the complaint, Apple once accused "OpenAI and its co-conspirators of engaging in a pattern of organised, institutional misconduct," which included io, but described it only as "a company co-founded by Mr. Tan and other former Apple executives." Apart from Tang Tan and Chang Liu, who are directly named, the filings make no further mention of Ive, Evans Hankey, or any other former Apple executives.

Although it's still too early to say whether Ive will be called to testify, the possibility is very real, particularly if OpenAI decides to deploy him to make things uncomfortable or embarrassing for Apple.

Such a turn of events would put Apple in an extraordinarily delicate position. Since leaving the company in 2019, Ive has publicly maintained a respectful stance towards Apple, and his appearances and interviews are typically carefully orchestrated.

These have included events attended alongside Laurene Powell Jobs, as well as his ongoing involvement with the Steve Jobs Archive. Earlier this year, Ive penned a personal letter for the archive's "Letters to a Young Creator" project, reflecting on his time working with Jobs.

Apple, for its part, appears to have reciprocated with equal respect, quietly re-examining several controversial decisions from Ive's final years at the company, including the MacBook butterfly keyboard. They clearly seem to be trying to keep both the lawsuit and Ive at a certain distance—which fits squarely with this approach.

But once the case enters the discovery phase, Apple will no longer have full control over who gets pulled in. Given that Ive founded io Products and oversaw the development of the hardware project in question, OpenAI could argue that he possesses relevant knowledge about how the product was developed, what information the team was working with, and whether Apple's trade secrets were involved.

Apple may then have to face an uncomfortable position: questioning Ive in court, challenging his account, or attempting to undermine the credibility of testimony from an executive who shaped many of its iconic products.

This would not be the first time Ive has testified in litigation involving Apple. In 2012, he was deposed for one of Apple's patent cases, answering questions about the company's design process and early iPhone and iPad prototypes.

However, appearing on the opposing side this time could strain the carefully maintained relationship between him and Apple, and there could even be friction between the two if Ive feels that OpenAI has unnecessarily dragged him into the dispute in a bid to pressure his former employer.

Do you think Jony Ive will be pulled into this lawsuit? Let us know your thoughts in the comments.
